19.history: The capital held Comhairle na Rìoghachd from the second year of the age, seated at a table too large for the room that held it, and every warrant, ruling and refusal of the kingdom went out from it. In the first summer the disbanded companies waited in its market square to be stood down, and sixty-one company rolls were carried into the vaults under the counting-house and bricked in. Niall was crowned here in the third year, Brìghde in the twenty-second and Eòghan in the twenty-eighth, and Mairead in the fifty-eighth; the bells of Òrd Mhacha rang a day and a night for Niall's death. The mint struck Bonn na Rìoghachd here from the fifth year, Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn kept its low grey office here, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean sat here until the twenty-seventh year, when it went to Cathair mhòr. The guild court heard the indentures and the yards' protests in its chambers. A second census was locked in the council's keeping-room in the thirty-third year and never aired. By the end of the age the lamps of its poorer wards burned shorter hours than the council's lighting order required, for want of coal at the price the order was written for.
19.known_for: the council's table, the mint, and the crownings

95.history: The harbour town where the council's word fixing Tìr-dhùthchais nan Tuathach was read aloud on the twenty-second of am Màrt in the first year, and where Walter Hale rendered it into the humans' tongue. In the second year the households met in the long room behind the harbour and opened Tional nan Tuathach's book, and Tional nan Tuathach sat here for the rest of the age: it voted grain against the winter, petitioned for the exchange of the cried-down coin, opened lifeboat and school purses, paid Cathair gheal's fine and Hannah Crane's, and kept its own minutes, counts and registers in the north. Walter Hale sat as its first speaker for thirty-one years and was buried in sight of its house in the thirty-third year; Mary Coyle followed him, the first woman in the chair, and Daniel Frayne after her. Its fishermen lost the southern grounds to the licence law of the thirtieth year. In the sixty-seventh year the room declined to send its books south to an Leabharlann, and the clerk entered two words, kept north.
95.known_for: Tional nan Tuathach, and the two words kept north

209.history: An inland town of the northern moss, on rush pasture the settled households were given because the better land nearer the coast was claimed. It buried more of its own in the first hungry winter than any town of the north, and its dead were named on a sheet in the church porch before Tional nan Tuathach had a book to name them in. Meal was carried to it from Caol mhòr on carts that sank to the hubs. In the fifteenth year Agnes Pike opened her school in a widow's byre here, with eleven scholars and no primer but the psalms and Cuimhne-coinneimh an Tionail, and moved it to the church porch each summer; Daniel Frayne walked in to it daily from Muileann leathan. Its weavers wove An Snàthainn Geal, into their cloth, and sold under their own mark from the fifty-fifth year. The wool mills raised here with Tional nan Tuathach's coin turned their first bolt in the fifty-ninth year, and Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's refusal to carry it brought the suit at Seann Bhral.
209.known_for: Agnes Pike's byre school and An Snàthainn Geal

27.history: The harbour below the capital on the lake shore, whose counting-house had come through the war with its shelves whole and whose garrison marched out under terms. In the third year Dùghall mac Iain took the humans' harbour-houses into the kingdom's keeping, and Ailean mac Iain spent eight months copying the humans' tariff out of eleven bound ledgers into Dia-thìris, saying exactly the old thing in the new tongue; the old tariff stood until the mint gave the council coin to take dues in. Its shipwrights took a guild charter in the fourteenth year and its guild court refused a Tuathaich rope-maker's plea in a single sitting. A shipwright of the town was the first name in an Leabharlann's reading-book. Its harbour clerk's corrected copy of Brìghde's crowning proclamation, Niall's name scored through, hangs under glass at the gate. In the thirty-sixth year its eldest masters lost their protest against Ros bheag's coal-ship yard before the guild court.
27.known_for: the tariff copied fair, and the proclamation under glass

330.history: A town of the north-western coast whose harbour officers sailed with the last ships and took their keys with them. In the second year its people opened the locked harbour store after Ceann mhòr and Cathair gheal did, and it is told that three women of the town drew up a reckoning of what was taken and by whom, so that the sharing could be answered for if anyone ever came to ask; no maor came. The old Rathad nan Cairtearan runs down to it from Cnoc ghorm and Àth fhada, and the wool trains of the forty-first year crossed the flooded low ground short of it in a cold rain, the carts finding their own way round the water. A household at a crossing near it kept one of the three lamps that lit the road by night. In the fifty-third year An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitched on the common near the town, and its magistrate licensed the acts as various, the fee paid.
330.known_for: the three women's reckoning, and An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn licensed as various

489.history: The humans' great harbour of the west, on the coast below the capes, where the fishing fleets still came in under a flag they had never learned to read and the old harbour bell rang the hours by a humans' clock. In the second year Ailean mac Iain found in its counting-house eleven district surveys behind a locked grating, every field about the town walked and numbered, and boxed them apart for the council; from them the shires were drawn. An Sireadh came home to its quay in the third year after sixteen days north-about and no land, and the priests of Manannan said over her return the prayer they had said over her going, that the sea be kept shut. Its innkeeper told Ailean of Niall's crowning. The ship lay careened here that winter. It is not the Seann Skell of the southern coast, where Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's Àrd-choimheadaiche sits, and the record keeps the two apart as west and south.
489.known_for: the district surveys, and An Sireadh's berth

143.history: The harbour of the north-west where a fisherman with a hammer and a bad temper broke the lock of the humans' harbour store in the second year, and the town, not the man, shared out rope, canvas and salt by the same rough justice that had shared a thin catch at Caol mhòr. Its fishermen traded in the broken store for two years on their own custom, and in the third year the council granted them a market right for the north-west coast, the smallest clause on Ailean's map of the shires and the one thing on it the town had already made true. Its first maor took the old human magistrate's house, which the town went on calling by its old name. In the fifteenth year Eilidh nic Leòid held her assize here in the heat of an t-Iuchar, heard nineteen causes to their ends and found fifteen for An Crùn; the Coombes and the Pettifers kept their ground on a custodian's countersign. Its timber yard took the order for Àth leathan's props in the thirty-ninth year.
143.known_for: the broken lock, and the seventeen suits

365.history: The market town of the middle country, seat of its own shire. Its courthouse burned in the last summer of the war, and when Coinneach mac Ailein, a custodian's younger son, came as its first maor in the fourth year he held his court under the market roof among the fish-scales. When a new courthouse was raised two years on he sat in it for exactly one sitting and moved back to the market hall the week after, and the two maoir who followed him did the same, until holding court under the scales became simply how justice was done in the town and no one thought to write down why. Ailean mac Iain had ridden no further north than its market before An Dealachadh, and he rode its letters to it again when the maoir were named. Its roll of arms and its dues were entered in the fourth year with the rest of the kingdom's.
365.known_for: the court held under the market roof

190.history: The larger harbour of the south coast struck by Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol in the fourth year. The wave broke its mole and carried its boats inland, so that when Ailean mac Iain came with the relief party the boats of the town lay among the barley and the harbour was gone. Its dead were carried up onto the rise behind the town, above the old harbour line, and buried through that first fortnight in ground the sea had not reached. An Crùn paid a third of the relief, the first time it had paid for anyone's loss. The town righted what boats it could and went back to fishing before the winter closed in. A generation later, in the twenty-seventh year, the harbour was opened again behind a new mole of dressed stone, and of the hulls the wave had cast into the fields one was found sound, caulked, and warped into the new harbour ahead of every boat built for it; the harbour-master keeps it moored at the quay-head as a relic.
190.known_for: the boats in the barley, and the boat kept for a relic

150.history: A township a little way inland on the south coast, on fields the sea had never in living memory reached, until Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol of the fourth year ran over its low ground and salted in one night what three generations had ploughed. The council moved its survivors to higher ground a mile inland before the winter closed the roads and paid for their seed from the treasury without a due asked, the first relief the restored kingdom granted anyone. The fields lay under salt for a generation. In the twenty-eighth year they bore again, and three households moved away after the wave, or their children in their place, asked for their old ground and were given it; the shire measured them back onto the same strips the humans' surveyors had cut, since those were the bounds the families still walked by memory. The chronicler entered its barley the night before word came of Brìghde's death.
150.known_for: the first relief, and the fields that bore again

364.history: A small town low on its shingle on the south coast, which gave its name to Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol of the fourth year, Tonn Mhòr Cnoc chaol. The water broke it in a single night before running on to Cuan dhearg and Achadh mhin. It was built again the following spring on the slope behind its old ground, high enough that the sea would have to climb a hill to trouble it a second time, and the old site was left as the water left it; the townsfolk call it an Tràigh Bhàthte, and do not build there. Its shepherds and those of Ros gharbh had summered their flocks time out of mind on the low island of Eilean mhin offshore, over which the wave also passed. Its houses were raised again faster than Ros gharbh's boats, a house wanting only hands and a boat wanting a builder.
364.known_for: the wave's name, and an Tràigh Bhàthte

282.history: The harbour of the west coast where the first humans came ashore generations before; a stone laid into the quay near the harbour-master's steps, worn nearly smooth, is still touched by children for luck. Households were walked north out of it under guard in the first year. An Sireadh sailed from it on the eleventh of an t-Ògmhios in the third year under Aonghas mac Mhurchaidh, a Cuan shean man, to seek An t-Aiseag north-about. Seumas Crùbach kept his shipwright's yard here, building frame first, and took Harry Marlow of Doire mhin on as a bound apprentice; when the guild charter reached the coast in the fourteenth year he tore the boy's indenture and kept him as a free hand at half wage, and other yards took up the rate. Harry measured a derelict human hull on the hard in his own book. The Cuan bheag lifeboat was built in its yard.
282.known_for: the first landing-stone, and Harry Marlow's torn indenture

5.history: A small inland town of the north, where the Pike family had ground grain since before An Dealachadh and the smith Joseph Marlow kept his forge. When the humans' coin was cried down in the fifth year, half the town brought its dead coin to Marlow, and he melted it and cast it into ploughshares and sold them back at the cost of the charcoal; the first furrow of that spring was cut with one of them by the last day of am Màrt. Walter Hale walked ten miles through snow to see it. The Tuathaich sang of Marlow after, that he turned the king's silence into iron and the iron into bread. Tional nan Tuathach took seed oats from the town's mill on credit in the first hungry year. Marlow's son Harry went from the forge to a shipwright's yard at Cuan shean, and sent his wage home each year; Agnes Pike, who opened the byre school at Doire ghlas, was a miller's daughter of the town.

166.history: A harbour town of the south-west coast, where the new coin was slower to come than almost anywhere in the kingdom. Its merchants did not wait on the mint: through the sixth year they traded in chits written on the paper of the house of Lia Fàil, whose name was old enough and trusted enough to stand in for coin, and when the coin came the chits were redeemed at the house's door, the house keeping back a tenth. A Ros bheag trader told Walter Hale that a tenth kept back by a name a man trusted was cheaper than a savings box kept by a name he did not. A priest of Òrd na Cloiche of the town heard the first reading of Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order. Its harbour court was well enough kept that Britheamhan na Cuairte's sitting there in the eighth year was brief.

431.history: The Seann Skell of the southern coast, not the harbour of the west, where Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's greatest house stands in a hall with blackened beams. In the sixth year Dòmhnall mac Thormoid was seated here as the first Àrd-choimheadaiche of Òrd Bhrìde, and here he wrote Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's first order of worship, read aloud near the end of am Faoilleach to eleven custodians and a scattering of hearth-keepers and a priest of Òrd na Cloiche; he kept every letter Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail sent or received in a plain ledger. From here went the copies of the order, and the refusals came back to it: Òrd an t-Seabhaig' letter of the sixth year and, in the thirty-fifth, the three-line letter refusing to own Raonaid nic Iain. In the forty-seventh year its council read Òrd an t-Seabhaig of Cnoc bheag their terms a seventh time, and they stood.
431.known_for: Àrd-choimheadaiche's house and the order of worship

20.history: A river town of the north-central country, heart of Òrd an t-Seabhaig's houses, whose altars answered to no custodian above them. In the sixth year the houses round it wrote to Seann Skell that Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order was handsome and not needed. The shire's arms carried a plain white billet from the fourth year for no reason any clerk could give, until the thirty-sixth, when a delegation of Òrd an t-Seabhaig asked for a hawk, and the maor broke the old die and pressed a white hawk among twelve crescents. An obelisk of unread script stands near it, which Una copied stroke by stroke in the thirty-second year and the council fenced against the cattle; its marks were laid beside those of Colbh Cnoc chiar and Calbh Cnoc ghorm by the students of Caol shean. By the forty-sixth year its river quays took in more grain in a season than the granaries of Cathair mhòr showed for a year.
20.known_for: Òrd an t-Seabhaig's country, the hawk on the seal, and Carragh Cnoc bheag

326.history: The southernmost of Òrd an t-Seabhaig's houses, close by the coast and far south of Cnoc bheag. It did not wait on the reading: in the sixth year it sent word to Seann Skell that it would take Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's written order entire, whatever it proved to be, and hung in its doorway a bell cast new for the purpose, the first bell any hawk-house had hung, to ring at Deas-ghnàth a' Ghuail's measured burnings. It rang it that summer at the burning of the year before a small crowd in the lane. Dòmhnall mac Thormoid wrote to it in his own hand, the first letter of thanks he composed in his office, and sent it a last copy of the order made with more care than any other. It became a house of Òrd Bhrìde, the one hawk-house of its kind.
326.known_for: the first bell hung in a hawk-house

26.history: A harbour town of the south-west, where Leabhar a' Chùraim of the old vein-house on the hill above the harbour was kept until the house closed it. Eilidh nic Leòid was born here and spent her whole working life in its counting-house and harbour court, copyist, recorder and at last justice in all but name. In the eighth year she was made circuit justice of the south-west and held her first assize here before she had properly left the town, measuring an orchard boundary with knotted cord. She set out from it with Murchadh Clàrc and a satchel of blank record-books, and it was here, within sound of the harbour, that she died in the sixteenth year with the gathered book of her rulings finished on the table by her bed. The fishing villages that feed its market lie along the coast road south from Seann Bhral.

47.history: The Seann Bhral of the west, on its harbour with the mud flats grey below the town wall and a scorpion carved over the old counting-house door that no one living can account for. Here on the ninth of an t-Sultain in the eighth year Eilidh nic Leòid gave Breith Leòid, that land held under human title passes to An Crùn and the working of it stays with the holders; it was cited in nearly every land case after. The western branch of Slighe a' Ghuail was carried to it in the thirteenth year. Its house of Manannan, reckoned the oldest on the coast, turned away Mary Coyle's eleven boats in the twenty-fifth year: the sea was the same, the house was not. Ruairidh mac Phàdraig ruled here in the fifty-ninth year that Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn is a carrier of An Crùn and must carry for any who pay, the first ruling Tional nan Tuathach won. Àth leathan's hewers sent their coal to its factors by cart from the sixty-ninth year.
47.known_for: Breith Leòid, and the ruling on Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn
